prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat with corticosteroids: oral corticosteroids are strongly advised against and IV methylprednisolone is not recommended [EAN_PNS_2023].
Do not delay admission and monitoring while waiting for the anti-GQ1b result.
Do not give IVIg directly after plasma exchange, and do not give a second IVIg course [EAN_PNS_2023, Walgaard_2021].
required_recommendations: IVIg and plasma exchange are not routinely advised in Miller Fisher syndrome; admit and monitor for limb weakness, bulbar or respiratory involvement or reduced consciousness [Leonhard_2019].

Repeat FVC, MIP and MEP and check bulbar function while symptoms progress; if limb weakness, bulbar or respiratory involvement develops, manage as GBS overlap, including IVIg or plasma exchange [EAN_PNS_2023].
Continuous cardiac telemetry with blood pressure monitoring while symptoms progress.
Fall precautions with assisted mobilisation (severe truncal ataxia, cannot sit unsupported) and DVT prophylaxis while mobility is limited.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Functional / metabolic brain imaging adds no value in a peripheral demyelinating syndrome.
Vascular imaging adds nothing once brain MRI with diffusion is normal: the deficit is bilateral and symmetric, with areflexia and no long-tract signs.

accepted: Miller Fisher syndrome (GBS variant), anti-GQ1b positive

differential.key_features: Shares anti-GQ1b with MFS, but needs reduced consciousness or hyperreflexia/extensor plantars; he is alert with complete areflexia, and the brain MRI is normal.
Raised in the ED, but the deficit is bilateral and symmetric with global areflexia and no crossed or long-tract signs, and diffusion-weighted MRI is normal.
Ophthalmoplegia with ataxia, but no confusion, no risk factor for thiamine deficiency, areflexia is not a feature, and MRI shows no periaqueductal or mammillary signal change.
Ptosis and ophthalmoplegia overlap, but areflexia, ataxia and sensory symptoms are not features of MG, and there is no fatigability.
Descending paralysis with bulbar weakness and dilated, poorly reactive pupils; here bulbar and limb strength are normal, pupils react, and sensory paraesthesias and ataxia are present.

key_clinical_evidence: Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia with normal limb strength and preserved alertness define Miller Fisher syndrome; the absence of limb weakness separates it from GBS [Wakerley_2014].

Anti-GQ1b IgG is found in most patients with Miller Fisher syndrome and supports, but does not by itself establish, the diagnosis; it is the antibody test advised when MFS is suspected [EAN_PNS_2023].
Brain MRI is recommended despite the typical syndrome to exclude posterior circulation stroke and Bickerstaff encephalitis.
Overlap syndromes (MFS extending to GBS or Bickerstaff encephalitis) occur: monitor for limb weakness, bulbar dysfunction or altered consciousness, which would change management.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Bilateral symmetric complete ophthalmoplegia and ptosis with global areflexia and no long-tract or crossed signs point to a peripheral cranial and spinal root disorder; the normal diffusion-weighted MRI excludes a brainstem infarct.
red_herrings.data_point: Initial ED suspicion of a posterior fossa stroke because of ophthalmoplegia and ataxia
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a vascular brainstem cause and miss Miller Fisher syndrome.

general.query: Miller Fisher syndrome course and management

results.finding: In Miller Fisher syndrome, IVIg and plasma exchange are not routinely advised because most patients recover fully within 6 months; patients are monitored for progression to GBS with limb weakness or to Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis.

Anti-GQ1b IgG is detected in most patients with Miller Fisher syndrome and in Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis; brain MRI is used to exclude structural brainstem lesions in patients with ophthalmoplegia and ataxia.

general.summary: Miller Fisher syndrome usually has a self-limiting course; immunotherapy is not routinely advised, and patients are monitored for overlap with GBS or Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis [Leonhard_2019, Wakerley_2014].

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL nerve conduction study. 1. Absent sural sensory nerve action potentials bilaterally; mildly reduced median sensory amplitudes. 2. Mildly prolonged distal motor latencies and borderline conduction velocities in median and peroneal motor nerves; CMAP amplitudes preserved. 3. Absent F-waves in bilateral peroneal nerves; borderline prolonged F-wave latencies in bilateral median nerves. 4. Absent H-reflex bilaterally. 5. Normal needle EMG. Sensory-predominant pattern with proximal conduction failure and preserved motor amplitudes.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required and 2 recommended actions, 1 red herring; Miller Fisher syndrome must be separated from brainstem stroke and Bickerstaff encephalitis, and managed without routine immunotherapy.

patient.chief_complaint: Four days of double vision, drooping eyelids and imbalance with falls in a 28-year-old man.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. D. is a 28-year-old previously healthy man presenting to the emergency department with a 4-day history of progressive neurological symptoms. Three weeks prior, he had a mild upper respiratory illness lasting 5 days. Four days ago, he noticed horizontal double vision that worsened rapidly. By day 2, he developed drooping of both eyelids. On day 3, he noticed severe balance problems: he fell twice and has been holding walls to walk. He denies any limb weakness: his arms and legs feel strong. He denies any headache, vomiting, or confusion. He has no back pain. He denies any recent travel or tick exposure. Emergency providers initially suspected a posterior fossa stroke given the ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. Brain CT was unremarkable.

neurological_exam.coordination: Severe truncal ataxia — cannot sit unsupported. Cannot perform tandem gait. Limb ataxia on finger-nose: severe dysmetria bilaterally with eyes open.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral complete ophthalmoplegia: cannot move eyes horizontally or vertically. Bilateral complete ptosis. Pupils equal and reactive to light. No facial weakness. Oropharyngeal function normal: no dysarthria, no dysphagia, gag intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Cannot walk without bilateral support. Severely ataxic.
neurological_exam.motor: Lower extremity strength 5/5 proximal and distal. Upper extremity 5/5 throughout.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Absent deep tendon reflexes bilaterally: complete areflexia throughout.
neurological_exam.sensory: Mild bilateral distal paresthesias. Vibration mildly reduced at great toes.
